title: What Is a SWIFT Code? A Beginner’s Complete Guide
summary: What is a SWIFT code and why does it matter for international transfers? Learn everything you need to know in this beginner-friendly, practical guide.

[Banking](https://blog.transfez.com/en/banking/)


You’re about to send money overseas, and the form asks for a “SWIFT code.” Cue the blank stare. What even is that? Is it the same as a routing number? Do you really need it, or can you just skip that field? If you’ve ever stared at an international transfer form feeling completely lost, you are not alone. This guide will break it all down in plain English so you never have to guess again. And if you’re regularly sending money between countries, understanding this one little code can save you a surprising amount of headache. If you want a head start on[how to find a SWIFT code](https://blog.transfez.com/en/swift-code-what-it-is-how-to-find-it/) , we’ve got you covered there too.

##


**What Is a SWIFT Code, Exactly?**


Let’s start from scratch. A **SWIFT code** is a unique identifier assigned to a bank or financial institution. It tells the international banking system exactly which bank should receive a transfer and, in some cases, which specific branch.


SWIFT stands for *Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication* . It’s a global network that connects thousands of banks across more than 200 countries. When you send money internationally, the SWIFT network is essentially the “highway” that routes your funds from bank A to bank B, safely and accurately.


###


**1. How Is a SWIFT Code Structured?**


A SWIFT code is made up of either 8 or 11 characters. Each section of the code carries specific information about the bank.


- **Characters 1-4:** The bank code, usually an abbreviation of the bank’s name.
- **Characters 5-6:** The country code, identifying where the bank is located (for example, “ID” for Indonesia or “SG” for Singapore).
- **Characters 7-8:** The location code, pointing to the bank’s city or head office.
- **Characters 9-11 (optional):** The branch code. If this part is missing or replaced with “XXX,” it refers to the bank’s primary office.


For example, a SWIFT code like *BANKIDJA* would break down into the bank’s name abbreviation, the country Indonesia, and the city Jakarta. Simple once you see the pattern.


###


**2. SWIFT Code vs. BIC: Are They the Same Thing?**


Yes, basically. You’ll sometimes hear the term *BIC* , which stands for *Bank Identifier Code* . SWIFT code and BIC are used interchangeably in most banking contexts. If a form asks for a BIC, you can enter your SWIFT code with confidence.


##


**Why Do You Need a SWIFT Code?**


Think of the SWIFT code as the GPS coordinates of a bank. Without it, your international transfer has nowhere to go. The banking system needs that code to route your money correctly across borders, currencies, and institutions.


###


**1. For Sending Money Internationally**


Whenever you transfer money to someone in another country, you will almost always need their bank’s SWIFT code. This applies whether you’re paying a freelancer abroad, sending support to family overseas, or settling a business invoice.


###


**2. For Receiving Money from Abroad**


If someone is sending money to your account from another country, they’ll need your bank’s SWIFT code. You’ll want to give them the correct code to avoid delays or failed transfers. If you’re an Indonesian based overseas and need to[transfer money from abroad to Indonesia](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-transfer-money-from-abroad-to-indonesia/) , make sure you have your Indonesian bank’s SWIFT code ready to share.


###


**3. For Wire Transfers and Payroll**


Companies paying international employees or contractors typically use wire transfers that require a SWIFT code. If you work abroad or receive a salary in a foreign currency, your employer’s finance team will almost certainly ask for this code.


##


**How to Find a SWIFT Code**


Good news: finding a SWIFT code is usually straightforward. Here are the most reliable ways to track one down.


1. **Check your bank’s website.** Most banks publish their SWIFT code prominently in the international transfers or help section of their site.
2. **Look at your bank statement.** Many banks print their SWIFT code directly on account statements or in the account details section of their app.
3. **Call or visit your bank.** If you’re not sure, your bank’s customer service team can give you the exact code, including the branch-specific version if needed.
4. **Use an online SWIFT code directory.** Several verified databases let you search by bank name and country. Just make sure you double-check any result against an official source before using it.


Always verify the code before you send. An incorrect SWIFT code can cause your transfer to bounce, get delayed, or even land in the wrong account.


##


**Common Mistakes People Make with SWIFT Codes**


Even savvy senders trip up sometimes. Here are the most common errors to avoid.


###


**1. Using the Head Office Code Instead of the Branch Code**


Some transfers require the specific branch code (the full 11-character version), not just the 8-character head office code. Always confirm with your recipient which version they need.


###


**2. Confusing SWIFT Codes with Other Codes**


A SWIFT code is not the same as a routing number (used in the US), a sort code (used in the UK), or a BSB number (used in Australia). Each country has its own local banking codes. SWIFT is the one that works internationally.


###


**3. Copying the Code Incorrectly**


It sounds obvious, but a single wrong character can derail your transfer. Always copy the code carefully and double-check it before hitting send. If you’re entering it manually, read it back letter by letter.


###


**4. Assuming Every Transfer Needs One**


Some modern remittance apps and platforms handle routing on the backend, meaning you might not need to enter a SWIFT code yourself. If you’re using a service designed for a specific corridor, like[sending money from Singapore to Indonesia in real time](https://blog.transfez.com/en/send-money-sg-to-id-real-time/) , the platform may already know the routing details. Check the instructions for whatever service you’re using.


##


**SWIFT Codes in the Context of Indonesian Banking**


For Indonesians living abroad or sending money back home, SWIFT codes are a regular part of life. Major Indonesian banks like BCA, Mandiri, BNI, and BRI all have their own SWIFT codes, and some have branch-specific versions too.


If you’re an Indonesian working overseas and want to[send money from abroad to Indonesia](https://blog.transfez.com/en/how-to-send-money-from-abroad-to-indonesia/) , your recipient’s bank SWIFT code is usually one of the first things you’ll need. Make sure to ask your family member or recipient to get this directly from their bank so you have the most accurate version.
